anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer reuses or chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite accurate statistics, producing inefficient access paths or join orders.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk pages or index structures causes data retrieval errors, missing/duplicate rows, or forced scan fall-backs.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, threads, or other OS objects prevent the database from allocating required resources, leading to partial or total service denial.

When these three root causes coexist, the database may exhibit erratic and hard-to-diagnose behavior: identical queries intermittently toggle between good and disastrous plans; some executions fail outright with OS-level ‘too many open files’ or ‘cannot map shared memory’ errors; others succeed but return wrong, missing, or duplicate rows due to corrupted indexes. Plan instability compounds the visibility of corruption—bad plans may unexpectedly bypass damaged indexes via full scans, masking inconsistencies, while resource-limit failures interrupt index rebuilds or statistics collection, prolonging exposure. Administrators may observe a swirl of symptoms: sudden performance cliff-drops, exploding I/O from scan fallbacks, sporadic session or worker creation failures, checksum or page-verification errors in engine logs, and wide variance between estimated and actual row counts as the optimizer is misled by silently corrupted structures.

Causally, the resource-limit anomaly can impede routine maintenance (checksum verification, vacuum, or index rebuild jobs) and suppress parallelism, allowing latent block/index corruption to persist and spread. Corrupted indexes in turn mislead the optimizer, increasing the likelihood of terrible plan choices or forcing plan recompilations after repeated runtime errors. These mischosen plans may drastically inflate memory, file-handle, or thread consumption, accelerating exhaustion of already tight OS limits and triggering further allocation failures. The feedback loop between plan mis-selection, structural corruption, and OS resource starvation amplifies performance volatility, data correctness risks, and availability outages far beyond what any single anomaly would cause in isolation.

entry.official_definition: Terminates any session that has been idle, but not within an open transaction, for longer than the specified amount of time.
entry.trigger_condition: A session is idle and not inside an open transaction longer than the configured threshold.
entry.workload_impact: The session is terminated; the documentation warns about using this with connection pools or middleware.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
